title: حِكَايَةُ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 903–904 (Night 218, continuing nights-217), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 218 continues the tale of Qamar al-Zamān. The king rides out to hunt and leaves his two sons to judge in his place, a day each. On the first day al-Amjad, Budūr's son, sits in judgement; and Ḥayāt al-Nufūs, the mother of al-Asʿad, writes to him declaring her love: a letter in rhymed prose closed by a couplet, saying that all the paper in the world could not hold her longing. She wraps it in perfumed silk with the braids of her hair and sends it by a eunuch to al-Amjad; and morning overtakes Shahrazād. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الثَّامِنَةَ عَشَرَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَتَيْنِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-thāminata ʿashara baʿda al-miʾatayni
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the eighteenth after the two-hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the two hundred and eighteenth night,
sentences.n: al-thāminata ʿashara, “eighteenth”: as in the nights before, the print has the masculine عشر where Classical Arabic would make it feminine (ʿashrata) to agree with the night; it is vocalised as printed. The ئ of المائتين is printed.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ الْمَلِكَ تَوَجَّهَ إِلَى الصَّيْدِ وَالْقَنَصِ وَأَمَرَ وَلَدَيْهِ أَنْ يَجْلِسَا فِي مَوْضِعِهِ لِلْحُكْمِ كُلُّ وَاحِدٍ يَوْمًا عَلَى عَادَتِهِمَا
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-malika tawajjaha ilā al-ṣaydi wa-al-qanaṣi wa-amara waladayhi an yajlisā fī mawḍiʿihi li-al-ḥukmi kullu wāḥidin yawman ʿalā ʿādatihimā
sentences.l: She-said: It-has-reached-me, O fortunate king, that the-king set-out to the-hunting and-the-chase, and-ordered his-two-sons that they-two-sit in his-place for-the-judging, each one a-day, according-to their-custom.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that the king rode out to hunt and chase game, and ordered his two sons to sit in his place and judge, each of them on his own day, as they were accustomed.
sentences.n: Shahrazād takes up the last sentence of the night before almost word for word; this time the print has no منهما, “of the two”, after kullu wāḥidin. The king is Qamar al-Zamān; his two sons are al-Amjad, born to Budūr, and al-Asʿad, born to Ḥayāt al-Nufūs. The shadda of توجّه is printed. li-al-ḥukmi: li- of purpose, “for judging”. kullu wāḥidin yawman, “each one a day”, is tacked on loosely, without a verb. ʿalā ʿādatihimā, “according to their custom”: ʿalā of conformity.

sentences.t: فَجَلَسَ لِلْحُكْمِ فِى الْيَوْمِ الْأَوَّلِ الْأَمْجَدُ بْنُ الْمَلِكَةِ بُدُورَ فَأَمَرَ وَنَهَى وَوَلَّى وَعَزَلَ وَأَعْطَى وَمَنَعَ
sentences.tr: fa-jalasa li-al-ḥukmi fī al-yawmi al-awwali al-Amjadu ibnu al-malikati Budūra fa-amara wa-nahā wa-wallā wa-ʿazala wa-aʿṭā wa-manaʿa
sentences.l: And-sat for-the-judging on the-day the-first al-Amjad, son (of) the-queen Budūr, and-he-commanded and-forbade, and-appointed and-dismissed, and-gave and-withheld.
sentences.i: On the first day al-Amjad, the son of Queen Budūr, sat in judgement; he commanded and forbade, appointed and dismissed, gave and withheld.
sentences.n: The verb comes first and its subject, al-Amjad, only after the phrases of purpose and time. The print spells fī with ى here, فى. ibn is written without its alif, بن, as between two names in a lineage; here the second name is his mother's. The three pairs of opposites are the stock picture of a ruler exercising his full authority: amara wa-nahā, “commanded and forbade”; wallā wa-ʿazala, “appointed (to office) and dismissed”, wallā being Form II of w-l-y, its shadda printed; aʿṭā wa-manaʿa, “gave and withheld”.

sentences.t: فَكَتَبَتْ لَهُ الْمَلِكَةُ حَيَاةُ النُّفُوسِ أُمُّ الْأَسْعَدِ مَكْتُوبًا تَسْتَعْطِفُهُ فِيهِ وَتُوضِحُ لَهُ أَنَّهَا مُتَعَلِّقَةٌ وَمُتَعَشِّقَةٌ فِيهِ وَتَكْشِفُ لَهُ الْغِطَا وَتُعْلِمُهُ أَنَّهَا تُرِيدُ وِصَالَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-katabat lahu al-malikatu Ḥayātu al-Nufūsi ummu al-Asʿadi maktūban tastaʿṭifuhu fīhi wa-tūḍiḥu lahu annahā mutaʿalliqatun wa-mutaʿashshiqatun fīhi wa-takshifu lahu al-ghiṭā wa-tuʿlimuhu annahā turīdu wiṣālahu
sentences.l: And-wrote to-him the-queen Ḥayāt al-Nufūs, (the) mother (of) al-Asʿad, a-written-thing, seeking-his-tenderness in-it, and-making-plain to-him that-she (is) attached and-enamoured in-him, and-uncovering for-him the-cover, and-making-him-know that-she wants his-union.
sentences.i: And Queen Ḥayāt al-Nufūs, the mother of al-Asʿad, wrote him a letter in which she pleaded for his tenderness, made plain that she was bound to him and in love with him, drew back the veil, and let him know that she wanted him in her bed.
sentences.n: Ḥayāt al-Nufūs writes to al-Amjad, her husband's son by his other wife: the stepmother's passion is what sets the tale that follows in motion. maktūb, “a written thing”, is the ordinary later word for a letter. tastaʿṭifuhu, Form X of ʿ-ṭ-f, “to seek someone's sympathy, plead with him”; fīhi, “in it”, is the letter. The four imperfects, tastaʿṭifu, tūḍiḥu, takshifu, tuʿlimu, describe the letter as she writes it. mutaʿalliqa, Form V participle, “attached”, and mutaʿashshiqa, Form V, “enamoured”, share one fīhi, “in him”, where Classical would attach mutaʿalliqa with bi-. kashafa al-ghiṭāʾ, “to lift the cover”, to speak openly; the print spells al-ghiṭāʾ without its final hamza, الغطا, as it often does with words in -āʾ. tuʿlimuhu, Form IV, “to inform”. wiṣāl, “union”, here bodily union, as in the night before.

sentences.t: فَأَخَذَتْ وَرَقَةً وَكَتَبَتْ فِيهَا هٰذِهِ السَّجَعَاتِ
sentences.tr: fa-akhadhat waraqatan wa-katabat fīhā hādhihi al-sajaʿāti
sentences.l: And-she-took a-sheet and-wrote in-it these rhymed-phrases:
sentences.i: She took a sheet of paper and wrote on it these lines of rhymed prose:
sentences.n: The print has هذة, a misprint for هذه, corrected here. sajaʿāt, plural of sajʿa, “a rhymed phrase”: the word for the rhymed prose (sajʿ) that follows, in which each clause ends on the rhyme of its neighbour; the print marks the clauses off with stars. A noun of the pattern faʿla takes an extra a in its plural: sajʿa, sajaʿāt.

sentences.t: مِنَ الْمِسْكِينَةِ الْعَاشِقَهْ * الْحَزِينَةِ الْمُفَارِقَهْ * الَّتِي ضَاعَ بِحُبِّكَ شَبَابُهَا وَطَالَ فِيكَ عَذَابُهَا *
sentences.tr: mina al-miskīnati al-ʿāshiqah * al-ḥazīnati al-mufāriqah * allatī ḍāʿa bi-ḥubbika shabābuhā wa-ṭāla fīka ʿadhābuhā *
sentences.l: From the-poor-one, the-loving-one, * the-sorrowing-one, the-parted-one, * who has-gone-to-waste through-love-of-you her-youth, and-has-grown-long in-you her-torment. *
sentences.i: From the poor woman who loves you, * the grieving woman parted from you, * whose youth has wasted away for love of you, and whose torment over you has been long. *
sentences.n: The letter opens, as letters do, with its sender: min, “from”. al-ʿāshiqah, al-mufāriqah: the print spells the feminine ending of these two rhyme words with ه rather than ة, and they are pointed here with the pausal sukūn that the spelling reflects (-ah). The rhymes: al-ʿāshiqah / al-mufāriqah, then shabābuhā / ʿadhābuhā. mufāriqa, Form III participle of f-r-q, “one parted (from the beloved)”. ḍāʿa, “to be lost, go to waste”. bi-ḥubbika: bi- of cause, “through love of you”. fīka, “in you”: fī of cause, “over you, on your account”. allatī ḍāʿa … shabābuhā: the verb stands before its subject, and -hā, “her”, ties the clause back to the woman.

sentences.t: وَلَوْ وَصَفْتُ لَكَ طُولَ الْأَسَفِ * وَمَا أُقَاسِيهِ مِنَ اللَّهَفِ * وَمَا بِقَلْبِي مِنَ الشَّغَفِ * وَمَا أَنَا فِيهِ مِنَ الْبُكَاءِ وَالْأَنِينِ * وَتَقَطُّعِ الْقَلْبِ الْحَزِينِ * وَتَوَالِى الْغُمُومِ * وَتَتَابُعِ الْهُمُومِ * وَمَا أَجِدُهُ مِنَ الْفِرَاقِ * وَالْكَآبَةِ وَالِاحْتِرَاقِ * لَطَالَ شَرْحُهُ فِى الْكِتَابِ * وَعَجَزَتْ عَنْ حَصْرِهِ الْحُسَّابُ *
sentences.tr: wa-law waṣaftu laka ṭūla al-asafi * wa-mā uqāsīhi mina al-lahafi * wa-mā bi-qalbī mina al-shaghafi * wa-mā anā fīhi mina al-bukāʾi wa-al-anīni * wa-taqaṭṭuʿi al-qalbi al-ḥazīni * wa-tawālī al-ghumūmi * wa-tatābuʿi al-humūmi * wa-mā ajiduhu mina al-firāqi * wa-al-kaʾābati wa-al-iḥtirāqi * la-ṭāla sharḥuhu fī al-kitābi * wa-ʿajazat ʿan ḥaṣrihi al-ḥussābu *
sentences.l: And-if I-described to-you (the) length (of) the-grief, * and-what I-endure-it of the-anguish, * and-what (is) in-my-heart of the-passion, * and-what I (am) in-it of the-weeping and-the-moaning, * and-(the)-breaking-to-pieces (of) the-heart the-sorrowing, * and-(the)-following-one-on-another (of) the-griefs, * and-(the)-succession (of) the-cares, * and-what I-find-it of the-parting, * and-the-gloom and-the-burning, * then-would-grow-long its-setting-out in the-letter, * and-would-fall-short of its-counting the-reckoners. *
sentences.i: Were I to describe to you how long my sorrow has lasted, * the anguish I endure, * the passion in my heart, * the weeping and moaning I am sunk in, * the breaking of my grieving heart, * the griefs that crowd one on another, * the cares that follow each on each, * and all I feel of parting, * of gloom and burning, * the telling would outrun any letter, * and the reckoners would fail to count it. *
sentences.n: The print has اجدة, a misprint for اجده, corrected here. The print has حصرة, a misprint for حصره, corrected here. The rhymes run in pairs and threes: al-asaf / al-lahaf / al-shaghaf; al-anīn / al-ḥazīn; al-ghumūm / al-humūm; al-firāq / al-iḥtirāq; al-kitāb / al-ḥussāb. law … la-ṭāla, “if … it would grow long”: the unreal condition, with la- on the answer. Everything between is the object of waṣaftu: ṭūla al-asafi, then the mā-clauses, “what …”, each with min, “of”, naming what the “what” is, and the nouns joined to them. -hi in uqāsīhi and -hu in ajiduhu go back to mā. uqāsī, Form III, “to endure, suffer”. wa-mā anā fīhi, “what I am in”: the state she is in. tawālī, Form VI verbal noun of w-l-y, “following one upon another”; the print spells it with ى, وتوالى. The shadda of تقطّع is printed. ghumūm and humūm, “griefs” and “cares”, are a stock near-synonym pair. The ā of الكآبة is printed. -hu in sharḥuhu and ḥaṣrihi is all she has listed. wa-ʿajazat ʿan ḥaṣrihi al-ḥussābu, “and the reckoners would fall short of counting it”: al-ḥussāb is the plural of ḥāsib, “one who reckons”, and a broken plural takes the feminine verb. The same letters could be read al-ḥisāb, “reckoning”, but that masculine noun would leave the feminine verb unexplained; the print is unpointed here, so the reading is ours.

sentences.t: وَقَدْ ضَاقَتْ عَلَيَّ الْأَرْضُ وَالسَّمَاءُ * وَلَالِي فِي غَيْرِكَ أَمَلٌ وَلَارَجَاءٌ *
sentences.tr: wa-qad ḍāqat ʿalayya al-arḍu wa-al-samāʾu * wa-lā lī fī ghayrika amalun wa-lā rajāʾun *
sentences.l: And-indeed have-grown-narrow upon-me the-earth and-the-sky, * and-not for-me in other-than-you a-hope and-not an-expectation. *
sentences.i: Earth and sky have closed in on me, * and I have no hope in anyone but you, and nothing else to look to. *
sentences.n: ḍāqat ʿalayya, “has grown narrow upon me”: has hemmed me in; ʿalā marks the one who suffers it, and the shadda of عليّ is printed. The phrase recalls the Qurʾān's “the earth, for all its breadth, grew narrow for them” (Q 9:118). The verb is feminine to agree with al-arḍ, the nearer subject. The print runs wa-lā lī and wa-lā rajāʾun together as ولالي and ولارجاء; both are kept as set. lā … wa-lā, “neither … nor”; lī, “for me”, is how Arabic says “I have”. fī ghayrika, “in other than you”: fī marks where hope is placed. amal and rajāʾ, “hope” and “expectation”, are another near-synonym pair. The rhyme: al-samāʾ / rajāʾ; the ء of both is printed.

sentences.t: فَقَدْ أَشْرَفْتُ عَلَى الْمَوْتِ * وَكَابَدْتُ أَهْوَالَ الْفَوْتِ * وَزَادَ بِي الِاحْتِرَاقُ * وَأَلَمُ الْهَجْرِ وَالْفِرَاقِ *
sentences.tr: fa-qad ashraftu ʿalā al-mawti * wa-kābadtu ahwāla al-fawti * wa-zāda bī al-iḥtirāqu * wa-alamu al-hajri wa-al-firāqi *
sentences.l: For I-have-looked-down upon the-death, * and-I-have-suffered (the) terrors (of) the-passing-away, * and-has-increased in-me the-burning * and-(the)-pain (of) the-forsaking and-the-parting. *
sentences.i: For I have come to the brink of death, * and suffered the terrors of slipping away; * the burning has grown in me, * and the pain of being shunned and parted. *
sentences.n: ashrafa ʿalā, Form IV, “to look down upon”, and so “to be on the verge of”. kābada, Form III, “to endure, wrestle with”. fawt, “passing, slipping away”: of life itself, or of the chance of the beloved; it is chosen to rhyme with al-mawt. zāda bī, “increased in me”: bi- marks the one in whom it grows. Two subjects share the verb zāda: al-iḥtirāqu, “the burning”, and alamu, “the pain”. hajr, “forsaking”, being shunned by the beloved. The rhymes: al-mawt / al-fawt; al-iḥtirāq / al-firāq.

sentences.t: وَلَوْ وَصَفْتُ مَا عِنْدِي مِنَ الْأَشْوَاقِ * مَا وَسِعَتْهَا الْأَوْرَاقُ *
sentences.tr: wa-law waṣaftu mā ʿindī mina al-ashwāqi * mā wasiʿathā al-awrāqu *
sentences.l: And-if I-described what (is) with-me of the-longings, * not would-have-room-for-them the-sheets. *
sentences.i: Were I to describe all the longing that is in me, * no pages could hold it. *
sentences.n: After law the answer here is negated with mā alone, without la-: mā wasiʿathā. wasiʿa, “to have room for, hold”. -hā, “them”, refers to the longings: a broken plural takes a feminine singular pronoun. mā ʿindī, “what is with me”, what I have. The rhyme: al-ashwāq / al-awrāq.

sentences.t: وَمِنْ كَثْرَةِ الْبَلْوَى وَالنُّحُولِ هَا أَنَا أُنْشِدُ وَأَقُولُ
sentences.tr: wa-min kathrati al-balwā wa-al-nuḥūli hā anā unshidu wa-aqūlu
sentences.l: And-from (the) abundance (of) the-affliction and-the-wasting, here I recite and-say:
sentences.i: And out of all my affliction and wasting, here I recite these lines:
sentences.n: min of cause, “from, because of”. nuḥūl, “wasting away”, the lover's stock malady. hā anā, “here I am”: hā points to what is present. unshidu wa-aqūlu, “I recite and say”, is the usual lead-in to verse. The rhyme carries through to the end of the prose: al-nuḥūl / aqūl.

sentences.t:
لَوْ كُنْتُ اَشْرَحُ مَا الْقَاهُ مِنْ حُرَقِ * وَمِنْ سَقَامٍ وَمِنْ وَجْدٍ وَمِنْ قَلَقِ
لَمْ يَبْقَ فِى الْاَرْضِ قِرْطَاسٌ وَلَا قَلَمٌ * وَلَا مِدَادٌ وَلَا شَيْءٌ مِنَ الْوَرَقِ
sentences.tr:
law kuntu ashraḥu mā alqāhu min ḥuraqi * wa-min saqāmin wa-min wajdin wa-min qalaqi
lam yabqa fī al-arḍi qirṭāsun wa-lā qalamun * wa-lā midādun wa-lā shayʾun mina al-waraqi
sentences.l:
If I-were setting-out what I-meet of burnings, * and-of sickness and-of ardour and-of unrest,
not would-remain on the-earth a-sheet nor a-pen, * nor ink, nor a-thing of the-paper.
sentences.i:
Were I to set out the burning pains I meet, * the sickness, the ardour and the unrest,
there would be left on earth no parchment and no pen, * no ink, no scrap of paper.
sentences.n: The verses are pointed in the print and copied as printed. The metre is basīṭ, and the lines rhyme in -aqi: ḥuraqi, qalaqi, waraqi; the first line rhymes within itself as an opening line often does. The print writes ashraḥu and alqāhu with a bare alif, اَشْرَحُ and الْقَاهُ, the hamza unwritten, and al-arḍ as الْاَرْضِ. law kuntu ashraḥu, “if I were explaining”: kāna with an imperfect after law. ḥuraq, plural of ḥurqa, “burning”; the print gives it a plain kasra, ḥuraqi, at the end of the half-line. The answer to law is negated with lam and no la-: lam yabqa, “there would not remain”. qirṭās, “a sheet (of paper or parchment)”; midād, “ink”. The couplet says, in verse, what the prose has just said: all the paper in the world would not be enough.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْمَلِكَةَ حَيَاةَ النُّفُوسِ لَفَّتْ تِلْكَ الْوَرَقَةَ فِي رُقْعَةٍ مِنْ غَالِى الْحَرِيرِ مُضَمَّخَةٍ بِالْمِسْكِ وَالْعَبِيرِ وَوَضَعَتْ مَعَهَا جَدَائِلَ شَعْرِهَا الَّتِي تَسْتَغْرِقُ الْأَمْوَالَ بِسِعْرِهَا
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-malikata Ḥayāta al-Nufūsi laffat tilka al-waraqata fī ruqʿatin min ghālī al-ḥarīri muḍammakhatin bi-al-miski wa-al-ʿabīri wa-waḍaʿat maʿahā jadāʾila shaʿrihā allatī tastaghriqu al-amwāla bi-siʿrihā
sentences.l: Then the-queen Ḥayāt al-Nufūs wrapped that sheet in a-patch of (the) costly (of) the-silk, steeped with-the-musk and-the-ʿabīr, and-put with-it (the) braids (of) her-hair, which swallow-up the-fortunes by-their-price.
sentences.i: Then Queen Ḥayāt al-Nufūs wrapped the sheet in a piece of the costliest silk, steeped in musk and sweet ʿabīr, and laid beside it the braids of her hair, whose price would swallow up fortunes.
sentences.n: ruqʿa, “a patch, a piece (of cloth)”. min ghālī al-ḥarīri, “of the costly of silk”: an adjective put before its noun in an iḍāfa, “the costliest silk”; the print spells ghālī with ى. muḍammakha, Form II participle, “smeared, steeped (in perfume)”, agrees with ruqʿa; its shadda is printed. bi-al-miski: bi- marks what it is steeped in. ʿabīr, a perfume of mixed scents, saffron among them. The narrative itself falls into rhyme here: al-ḥarīr / al-ʿabīr, shaʿrihā / siʿrihā. The ئ of جدائل is printed. allatī, “which”, refers to the braids, a plural of things taking a feminine singular. tastaghriqu, Form X, “to take up wholly, swallow up”; bi-siʿrihā, “by their price”: bi- of means. A lock or braid of the beloved's hair is a lover's token, and a woman's long braids were prized.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ لَفَّتْهَا بِمِنْدِيلٍ وَأَعْطَتْهَا لِخَادِمٍ وَأَمَرَتْهُ أَنْ يُوصِلَهَا إِلَي الْمَلِكِ الْأَمْجَدِ
sentences.tr: thumma laffathā bi-mindīlin wa-aʿṭathā li-khādimin wa-amarathu an yūṣilahā ilā al-maliki al-Amjadi
sentences.l: Then she-wrapped-it with-a-kerchief, and-gave-it to-a-servant, and-ordered-him that he-convey-it to the-king al-Amjad.
sentences.i: Then she wrapped it all in a kerchief, gave it to a eunuch, and ordered him to carry it to King al-Amjad.
sentences.n: -hā, “it”, is the sheet with all that is wrapped around it. The shadda of لفّت is printed. bi-mindīlin, “with a kerchief”: bi- marks what she wraps it in. aʿṭathā li-khādimin: the later language marks the receiver with li-, where Classical would give aʿṭā two objects. khādim, “servant”: in a palace, and in the women's quarters especially, usually a eunuch. awṣala, Form IV, “to convey, deliver”. The print spells ilā with a dotted yāʾ here, الي. al-Amjad is called king because he sits in his father's place that day.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the-morning overtook Shahrazād, and-she-fell-silent from the-permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The closing formula, as at the end of every night. The rhyme falls on al-ṣabāḥ / al-mubāḥ.
